Abstract
Di Zi Gui
, a Qing-era moral primer, is discussed in contemporary Chinese family education, school moral education, and classical-recitation initiatives. Existing accounts document heterogeneous uses but do not establish their current prevalence or effects on children’s autonomy. This Hypothesis and Theory article develops a conditional model through close reading of 34 purposively selected precept groups from one modern working edition and comparison with psychological research from other contexts. Textual evidence, theoretical inference, and predictions requiring empirical testing are distinguished throughout. Adultcentrism identifies a possible asymmetry in interpretive authority; self-determination theory supplies the core distinction between controlled compliance and endorsed commitment. The proposed developmental focus is middle childhood, approximately 8–12 years, without assuming that findings from other age groups transfer directly. Three candidate pathways concern the permitted form of action, the motivational basis of conformity, and the legitimacy and expression of affect: behavioral standardization, compliance reinforcement, and emotional suppression

Existing scholarship can be grouped into four overlapping bodies. Textual and historical studies examine authorship, editions, structure, sources, and circulation (

8. Discussion and testable propositions
8.1. Contributions and boundary conditions
The contribution is a conditional research framework, not a finding that the primer diminishes autonomy. It complements
Luo and Yang (2026)
and
Santana (2026)
by linking a specified text to enactment, child reception, and differentiated psychological hypotheses. The core theoretical contrast is between nonreciprocal interpretive authority and the conditions under which commitments can be understood and endorsed. Psychological control and emotion invalidation identify candidate processes; they do not convert textual analysis into outcome evidence. Behavioral structure, active filial identification, and prosocial benefit remain genuine alternatives rather than concessions added after a predetermined critical conclusion (
Deci and Ryan, 2000
;
Shek and Law, 2019
).
The primary comparison must be tested directly. An exposure-only model should include contact frequency, duration, and setting, alongside prespecified background covariates and baseline outcomes. An expanded model should add independently assessed enactment, and then reception of specific instructional episodes. Incremental explanatory va

[... bounded source excerpt ...]

rmat. These steps would test the model rather than retrospectively confirm a conclusion already attributed to the text.
9. Conclusion
Di Zi Gui
provides material for a conditional psychological model, not evidence that its readers experience diminished autonomy. The present analysis distinguishes textual affordances, interpretation, enactment, reception, candidate mechanisms, and possible outcomes. It proposes that restrictions on action form, pressure sustaining conformity, and moral disqualification of affect may matter under specified conditions. Children’s meaning-making and the text’s resources for care, reciprocity, remonstrance, and inquiry also make other pathways conceivable.
The autonomy at issue is relational and culturally situated, compatible with endorsed filial obligations but not reducible to outward obedience. For the proposed middle-childhood focus, the testable question is whether enactment and reception improve prediction beyond exposure, and whether the differentiated processes survive discriminant, longitudinal, and contextual tests. P4C offers one possible moderator only where interpretive participation is consequential. Without child accounts and enactment observations, the model remains an agenda for empirical inquiry.
